stimulus.text:
The Security Council as designed in the United Nations Charter, signed June 26, 1945.

| Members | Who they were | Power |
| 5 permanent members | United States, Soviet Union, Britain, France, China | Any one could veto a Council decision |
| 6 rotating members | Elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms | Voted, but held no veto |
stimulus.source_note: Table drawn from the design of the United Nations Charter (San Francisco, June 1945): five permanent members with the veto and six elected members in the original Council. The elected membership grew to ten in 1965.

source: original; stimulus drawn from book-grounded paraphrases, tables, and photographs (see source_note)
stem: Why did the founders give the great powers a veto in the Security Council?

options.text: To keep the great powers inside the United Nations, unlike the League
To let the great powers run the General Assembly as well
options.misconception: The General Assembly gave every member one vote, and the veto applied only in the Security Council.

options.text: To give small nations a stronger voice than large ones
options.misconception: The veto strengthened the great powers, not the small nations.

options.text: To let the Council declare war without any debate
options.misconception: The veto limited the Council's power; it did not let the Council rush into war.

rationales.A: The League of Nations had failed partly because great powers stayed out or walked away, so the veto promised them that the United Nations could never act against their will.
rationales.B: Background from the books: the General Assembly gave every member one vote, and the veto applied only in the Security Council.
rationales.C: Background from the books: the veto strengthened the great powers, not the small nations.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the veto limited the Council's power; it did not let the Council rush into war.
rationales.general:
1. The table shows five permanent members, each able to veto a Council decision.
2. Background: the League of Nations had failed when the United States never joined and other great powers left.
3. The founders believed the new organization would fail the same way if a great power could be outvoted on war and peace.
4. The veto was the price of keeping the great powers in the room, even though it could freeze the Council.
Remember: institutions built to keep the powerful inside often give them a way to say no.
